n: A leading Pharisee invites Jesus for a Sabbath meal, but the guests are watching Him closely, looking for something to criticize.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for sharing a meal.

n: A man suffering from dropsy is right in front of Him — perhaps placed there as a test.

f.g: Edema — painful swelling from fluid buildup, often a sign of serious illness.

n: Jesus asks the experts directly: does the law allow healing on the Sabbath?

f.g: Permitted by the law of Moses.

n: They stay silent. Jesus takes hold of the man, heals him, and sends him on his way.
He asks: if your son or ox fell into a well on the Sabbath, wouldn’t you rescue it right away? Mercy belongs on the Sabbath.

f.g: Some ancient manuscripts read “a son or an ox.”

n: They have no answer. The point is unanswerable: the Sabbath is for doing good.
Jesus notices guests jockeying for the best places near the host, and He tells a parable about it.

f.g: The places of honor at the table (not separate rooms).

n: At a wedding feast, don’t grab the seat of highest honor. A more distinguished guest might arrive.
The host might then ask you to give up your seat, and you’d have to move — embarrassed — to the lowest place, the only one left.
Instead, take the lowest seat. If the host moves you up, you’ll be honored in front of everyone. This echoes Proverbs.
The principle reaches beyond dinner parties: those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and the humble will be exalted.

f.w: whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased

n: Jesus then speaks to the host: don’t invite only friends, family, and rich neighbors who will repay you with invitations of their own.
Instead, invite those who can never repay — the poor, the disabled, the blind. Such people were often excluded from social life.
You will be blessed precisely because they can’t pay you back. God Himself will reward you at the resurrection of the righteous.
A guest piously remarks how blessed it will be to feast in God’s kingdom. Jesus uses this comment to ask whether they will actually accept the invitation.

f.w: eat bread in the kingdom of God
f.g: The Messianic banquet — a common Jewish image of the coming kingdom.

n: A man prepares a great banquet and sends out many invitations.

f.w: A certain man made a great supper

n: Custom was to send a first invitation, then a servant to announce when the meal was ready. Now the time has come: everything is ready.
Yet everyone makes excuses. The first says he must go see a field he bought — though no one buys land without inspecting it first.

f.g: All alike, as if by agreement.

n: Another says he has bought five pairs of oxen and needs to test them — another flimsy excuse for something that could wait.

f.g: Ten oxen — a sign of wealth.

n: A third says he just got married and can’t come. Good things — property, work, family — can crowd out God’s invitation.
The angry host sends his servant quickly into the town’s streets to bring in the poor, disabled, and blind — the very people Jesus just said to invite.
The servant reports it is done, but there is still room. God’s house has space for more.

f.g: Heaven has room for all who will come.

n: The master sends him beyond the town to the roads and hedges — a picture of the gospel going to the Gentiles. “Compel” here means to urge strongly, not to force.

f.g: Country roads and fences, where travelers and outcasts might be.
Urge them earnestly, overcoming their sense that they are unworthy.

n: Those who refused the invitation will not taste the feast. The door was open; they chose not to enter.

f.w: none of those men which were bidden

n: Huge crowds are following Jesus. He turns to tell them what following Him really requires.

f.g: Many were enthusiastic but hadn’t yet counted the cost.

n: “Hate” is a Hebrew way of saying “love less.” Devotion to Christ must come first, above even family and one’s own life. Matthew says “loveth more than me.”

f.g: A Semitic idiom of comparison: to love less, to put second.

n: A disciple must carry his own cross and follow — willing to suffer and even die for Christ.
Before building a tower, a wise person calculates whether he has enough resources to finish it.
Otherwise, he might lay the foundation and run out of money, becoming a laughingstock.
Onlookers will mock: he started but couldn’t finish. A half-hearted disciple is like an abandoned building project.
A king facing an army twice his size would carefully consider whether he could win before going to battle.
If not, he would send messengers early to negotiate peace. Discipleship requires that same clear-eyed reckoning.
The bottom line: anyone unwilling to give up everything cannot be Christ’s disciple. This means willingness to put all on the altar.

f.w: forsaketh not all that he hath

n: Salt is valuable, but salt that has lost its flavor is useless. Disciples who lose their distinctiveness lose their purpose.
Tasteless salt isn’t even useful as fertilizer — it’s just thrown out. Jesus closes with His call to truly listen.

f.g: Manure pile, used to fertilize fields.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear
